issues.legal_issue: The six-month period for notifying a landlord of succession to a permanent tenure or obtaining mutation is directory, and missing it does not permanently bar a successor’s suit to recover rent.
material_facts: The plaintiffs succeeded to a permanent tenure and brought a suit to recover arrears of rent.
They had not given the prescribed notice of succession within six months.
The courts below found that their names had been mutated in the landlords’ records; the Supreme Court proceeded on the assumption that the mutation had not occurred within six months.
The plaintiffs’ required succession steps had been performed by the time the rent claim was considered.
issues.conclusion: The six-month period is directory. Failure to comply within that period delays recovery by suit only until the required succession steps are performed; it does not permanently extinguish the right to sue, subject to limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 15 and 16 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, as amended by Bengal Act IV of 1928, a successor must notify the landlord of succession or obtain mutation, and may not recover rent by suit until the required duties have been performed. The six-month period in section 15 is directory rather than mandatory. Section 16 is penal and must be confined to its terms: its bar lasts only until performance of the required duties and cannot be extended by implication into a permanent bar. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.successor_rent_recovery_suit: A person who succeeded to a permanent tenure brought a suit to recover rent payable to that person as its holder.
predicates.succession_steps_not_completed_within_si: The successor did not give notice of succession or obtain mutation within six months of succession.
predicates.succession_steps_eventually_completed: The successor later performed the required steps to notify the landlord of succession or obtain mutation.

issues.definition: If a successor seeking rent through a suit completes the required succession steps after the six-month period, the suit is available once those steps are completed.

issues.legal_issue: Mutation in a landlord’s rent-roll may be proved by secondary evidence when the original rent-roll or a certified copy is unavailable.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought production of the landlords’ records concerning mutation, but those records were not produced.
Witnesses testified that the plaintiffs’ names had been mutated in the landlords’ offices and that rent was paid and accepted after mutation.
An order sanctioning mutation and a rent receipt were produced and proved.
The courts below accepted that evidence as proof of mutation.
issues.conclusion: The courts below were justified in finding that the plaintiffs had been mutated in the landlords’ rent-roll; mutation could be proved by the secondary evidence adduced.
issues.legal_principle: The fact of mutation, like any disputed fact, may be proved by the original rent-roll or its certified copy, and, if those are unavailable, by other secondary proof. The Court applied this evidentiary principle to the mutation requirement in section 15 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, as amended by Bengal Act IV of 1928. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.mutation_proof_dispute_in_rent_claim: A dispute in a rent claim concerns whether a successor’s name was entered in the landlord’s rent-roll.
predicates.rent_roll_records_not_produced: The original rent-roll or a certified copy was unavailable because the records were not produced.
predicates.secondary_mutation_evidence_adduced: Other evidence, such as testimony, a mutation order, or rent receipts following mutation, was presented to show that mutation occurred.

issues.definition: When mutation is disputed in a rent claim, the rent-roll records are not produced, and other evidence of mutation is presented, that evidence may prove mutation.
